title: Annual research review: Infant development, autism, and ADHD--early pathways to emerging disorders.

subsections.subsection_title: Overlapping Genetic, Cognitive, and Phenotypic Pathways Between ASD and ADHD
subsections.content:
Accumulating evidence supports substantial overlapping genetic, cognitive, and phenotypic pathways between autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), challenging traditional diagnostic boundaries. Twin studies have demonstrated moderate to high genetic correlations (r > 0.50) between autistic traits and ADHD behaviors in the general population, indicating shared heritable influences that extend across the full spectrum of symptom expression, not merely at clinical thresholds ref [2]. This aligns with a polygenic framework in which both disorders represent quantitative extremes of continuously distributed traits, rather than distinct categorical entities ref [1]. Cognitive profiles reveal overlapping deficits in executive functioning, attentional control, and social cognition, though with some domain-specific variations: for instance, both groups exhibit pragmatic language impairments, while structural language difficulties are more pronounced in ASD, particularly in early development ref [4]. Latent class analyses in clinical and population samples have identified subgroups with combined ASD-ADHD symptoms, suggesting a gradient model where comorbid presentations reflect greater neurocognitive impairment than either disorder alone ref [3]. Furthermore, adult studies using temperament and character inventories show similar endophenotypic profiles—such as low reward dependence and high harm avoidance—in both ASD and ADHD, reinforcing a shared neurobiological substrate ref [7].

Language impairments in both disorders, particularly pragmatic deficits, are prevalent and often indistinguishable in school-aged children, though distinct patterns emerge in preschoolers, where structural language delays are more common in ASD and SLI than in ADHD ref [4]. Importantly, the co-occurrence of ADHD symptoms in children with ASD is associated with greater overall language difficulty, suggesting interactive effects between attentional and social-communicative systems ref [4]. These findings collectively support a dimensional model of neurodevelopmental risk, wherein genetic and cognitive vulnerabilities converge across traditional diagnostic categories, necessitating transdiagnostic approaches to early identification and intervention.

subsections.subsection_title: Motor and Sensorimotor Development as Predictors of Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence underscores motor and sensorimotor development as critical early predictors of neurodevelopmental outcomes in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Infants at heightened risk for ASD exhibit subtle delays in fine motor skills as early as 12 months, which prospectively predict later expressive language deficits, even in those who do not receive an ASD diagnosis by age 36 months ref [11]. Similarly, oral- and manual-motor impairments in infancy and toddlerhood are strongly associated with reduced speech fluency in childhood, challenging assumptions that nonverbal communication is a matter of choice rather than capacity in ASD ref [8]. Meta-analytic synthesis confirms that motor coordination deficits are pervasive and substantial in ASD, with a large effect size (d = 1.20) across diverse motor domains, suggesting these are core, not ancillary, features ref [7]. Gestural impairments in ASD extend beyond general motor clumsiness, involving specific errors in action planning and spatial orientation that distinguish them from children with developmental coordination disorder or ADHD alone ref [9].

Prechtl’s assessment of general movements (GMs) provides a sensitive, noninvasive window into early nervous system integrity, with abnormal GM patterns—such as cramped-synchronized or absent fidgety movements—predicting later cerebral palsy and, increasingly, neurodevelopmental disorders including ASD and ADHD ref [10]. Population-based studies further reveal that early psychomotor delays, as documented in routine pediatric assessments, significantly predict later ASD and ADHD symptomatology, independent of other risk factors ref [13]. These findings collectively position sensorimotor development not merely as a correlate, but as a foundational pathway through which early neural dysregulation manifests and forecasts broader cognitive, communicative, and behavioral outcomes.

subsections.subsection_title: Role of Attention, Sensory Processing, and Social Orienting in Early Development
subsections.content:
Attentional orienting, sensory processing, and social orienting form foundational pillars of early neurodevelopment, with atypicalities in these domains serving as early markers for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Infants demonstrate an intrinsic coupling between motor activation and visual attention, where spontaneous gaze shifts are preceded by brief motor fluctuations, suggesting that embodied movement facilitates attentional engagement in the first months of life ref [12]. By 7 months, atypical visual orienting latencies—particularly prolonged saccadic reaction times—are linked to later ASD diagnosis and correlate with reduced microstructural integrity of the splenium of the corpus callosum, implicating posterior cortical circuits in early attentional dysfunction ref [8]. Infants at familial risk for ASD also show diminished neural sensitivity to dynamic eye gaze, as indexed by event-related potentials, which predicts social communication outcomes at 36 months ref [13].

In toddlers with ASD, attentional disengagement is markedly impaired, with some children remaining fixated on a central stimulus for the entire trial duration, a pattern resembling obligatory attention seen in typically developing 2-month-olds ref [9]. However, their sensitivity to directional eye cues remains intact when presented in controlled paradigms, suggesting that deficits lie not in low-level cue detection but in the modulation of attention by social context ref [14]. Contextual factors, such as the presence of child-directed speech and eye contact, critically influence attention allocation: in the absence of these dyadic cues, toddlers with ASD attend to social scenes similarly to controls, but show reduced face and lip monitoring when such cues are introduced ref [17]. Furthermore, neonatal sleep patterns predict later attentional orienting and distractibility, highlighting the role of early regulatory systems in shaping attentional trajectories ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: Temperament, Self-Regulation, and Environmental Influences on Early Risk
subsections.content:
Temperament and self-regulation emerge as critical early markers of neurodevelopmental risk, with distinct profiles observed in infants later diagnosed with ASD or ADHD. High-risk infants, particularly those with an older sibling with ASD, exhibit reduced Surgency and Effortful Control as early as 7 months, alongside elevated Negative Affect and reduced Cuddliness by 24 months, suggesting a temperament trajectory that precedes clinical diagnosis ref [20]. Similarly, infants who develop ASD show diminished Behavioral Approach and impaired Effortful Emotion Regulation, characterized by low positive affect, high negative affect, and poor attentional control, which are predictive of symptom severity even after controlling for IQ and sex ref [10]. In ADHD, reactive control and low Effortful Control are independently linked to hyperactivity-impulsivity and inattention, respectively, supporting a dual-pathway model where motivational and regulatory deficits contribute differentially to symptom expression ref [23], ref [24].

Environmental influences, particularly prenatal maternal stress, further modulate these temperamental trajectories, increasing risk for both autistic traits and ADHD behaviors in early childhood, with sex-specific effects observed in males and females ref [19]. Sleep disturbances in infancy also predict later ADHD diagnosis, especially when co-occurring with psychosocial stressors and bedtime struggles, highlighting the interplay between biological vulnerability and environmental context ref [26]. Parental responsiveness and early attentional capacities at 9 months predict later Effortful Control, underscoring the role of caregiving environments in shaping self-regulatory development ref [22]. Together, these findings indicate that temperament and self-regulation are not merely endophenotypes but dynamic constructs shaped by gene-environment interactions, offering a framework for early identification and targeted intervention.

subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Neurodevelopmental Markers of ASD and ADHD
subsections.content:
Early behavioral and neurodevelopmental markers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) emerge prominently within the first year of life, including atypical social orienting, reduced response to name, and delays in postural and motor milestones. Prospective studies demonstrate that failure to respond to name by 12 months of age is a highly specific indicator of later ASD, with specificity exceeding 0.89, though sensitivity remains moderate ref [10]. Infants later diagnosed with ASD also exhibit significant head lag during pull-to-sit at 6 months, a marker of impaired postural control that distinguishes them from low-risk peers ref [34]. Delays in sitting and standing, along with reduced infant-initiated posture changes, are evident as early as 6 to 14 months in high-risk infants, suggesting motor disruptions precede and potentially constrain social-communicative development ref [31].

Repetitive and atypical object exploration behaviors, such as spinning or unusual visual inspection of objects, are reliably observed at 12 months in infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis, often exceeding four standard deviations above typical levels ref [32]. These behaviors, alongside diminished social smiling, gaze avoidance, and hypoactivity, are detectable in retrospective analyses of home videos as early as 4–6 months, with movement disturbances identified via systematic motion analysis ref [30], ref [33]. In parallel, early markers of ADHD include reduced head circumference percentile at 3 and 18 months, delays in motor and language development, and difficult temperament by 9–18 months, alongside maternal factors such as advanced age and lower education ref [9]. Together, these findings indicate that ASD and ADHD each have distinct, yet partially overlapping, early behavioral signatures that manifest in sensorimotor, attentional, and regulatory domains during infancy, offering critical windows for early identification and intervention.

subsections.subsection_title: Clinical Overlap and Comorbidity in Neurodevelopmental Syndromes
subsections.content:
Clinical overlap between autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is increasingly recognized in neurodevelopmental syndromes, where comorbid presentations are more prevalent than in the general population. In neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), for instance, nearly 56% of children exhibit clinically significant ASD symptoms, with an additional 30–40% showing elevated ADHD traits, suggesting shared neurobiological vulnerabilities ref [35]. Similar patterns emerge in tuberous sclerosis complex, where ASD and ADHD co-occur in over 40% of cases, often with distinct behavioral profiles that complicate diagnostic delineation ref [2]. In 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, ADHD is the most common psychiatric comorbidity, yet nearly one-third of affected children also meet criteria for ASD, pointing to a common pathway of disrupted cortical connectivity and executive dysfunction ref [3]. These syndromes highlight that diagnostic boundaries are often fluid in the context of genetic etiologies, with symptom clusters reflecting underlying neural circuit disruptions rather than discrete disorders.

Furthermore, studies of fragile X syndrome and Rett syndrome reveal that ADHD-like hyperactivity and inattention frequently precede or coexist with core ASD features, challenging traditional categorical models ref [4]. The high rates of comorbidity across these syndromes support dimensional models of neurodevelopmental pathology, wherein genetic risk factors influence broad domains of social communication, attentional control, and behavioral regulation in overlapping ways ref [5]. This convergence underscores the need for syndrome-specific, transdiagnostic assessment frameworks that account for both primary genetic effects and secondary behavioral adaptations.

subsections.subsection_title: Neurodevelopmental Pathways in Autism and ADHD
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence supports the notion that autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) arise from overlapping neurodevelopmental pathways characterized by disruptions in early brain circuit formation. Genetic studies reveal that rare, penetrant variants—such as copy number alterations and single-gene mutations—can predispose individuals to both conditions, challenging traditional diagnostic boundaries and supporting the framework of developmental brain dysfunction, wherein distinct clinical phenotypes emerge from shared underlying neural disruptions ref [36]. Functional genomic analyses further pinpoint specific cell types and developmental windows of vulnerability; for instance, coexpression networks in the human midfetal cortex implicate deep-layer projection neurons in ASD pathogenesis, suggesting that aberrant cortical connectivity may originate during critical periods of neurogenesis and migration ref [37]. These disruptions may manifest differently across individuals due to genetic background and environmental modulation, leading to heterogeneous behavioral outcomes such as social communication deficits in ASD or attentional dysregulation in ADHD.

Moreover, longitudinal neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies indicate that early alterations in frontostriatal and default mode network maturation are common to both disorders, with subtle differences in timing and regional emphasis potentially determining diagnostic trajectory. The convergence of genetic risk, altered neuronal gene expression, and disrupted synaptic pruning during early postnatal development underscores a model in which ASD and ADHD are not discrete entities but rather points along a spectrum of neurodevelopmental perturbation, shaped by dynamic gene-environment interactions across the first years of life.

subsections.subsection_title: Compensatory Mechanisms and Early Behavioral Adaptations
subsections.content:
Infants and toddlers at risk for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often exhibit early behavioral adaptations that may reflect compensatory mechanisms in response to atypical neural processing. For instance, toddlers with elevated autism symptoms demonstrate slowed habituation to faces, suggesting a heightened attentional engagement or reduced neural efficiency in processing socially relevant stimuli, which may represent an adaptive strategy to extract meaningful social information despite underlying perceptual challenges ref [38]. These compensatory behaviors can manifest as increased visual fixation on eyes or mouth regions, potentially offsetting deficits in implicit social learning. Similar adaptive patterns are observed in attentional reorienting, where some children with emerging ASD show prolonged gaze maintenance to social stimuli, possibly as a strategy to compensate for impaired automatic attentional cueing ref [6]. In parallel, early motor and gestural adaptations—such as increased use of pointing or vocalizations—may serve to bridge communication gaps in the absence of typical language development ref [17]. These behavioral adaptations are not uniform and are modulated by individual differences in temperament, executive function, and caregiver responsiveness, highlighting the dynamic interplay between neurodevelopmental risk and environmental support.

Emerging evidence suggests that compensatory mechanisms in early development may buffer the expression of core symptoms, delaying clinical diagnosis but not necessarily altering long-term trajectories. For example, children with elevated ASD symptoms who exhibit stronger effortful control or heightened sensitivity to social feedback may develop more effective self-regulatory strategies, mitigating social withdrawal ref [15]. Caregiver-mediated interventions that reinforce these adaptive behaviors—such as contingent responsiveness and joint attention scaffolding—can further enhance developmental outcomes, underscoring the role of the caregiving environment in shaping compensatory pathways. However, these adaptations may come at a cognitive cost, as sustained attentional effort can lead to fatigue and reduced flexibility in novel contexts. Longitudinal studies are needed to disentangle whether such behaviors represent resilience or merely delayed manifestation of underlying neurobiological differences.

subsections.subsection_title: Role of Caregiver and Executive Function in Early Development
subsections.content:
The development of executive function (EF) in early childhood is profoundly influenced by caregiver behaviors and the quality of the caregiving environment. Maternal EF, including working memory and inhibitory control, has been shown to uniquely predict child EF development, independent of maternal education and child verbal ability, with these effects becoming more pronounced by 36 months of age ref [40]. Moreover, negative caregiving behaviors—such as intrusiveness or low responsiveness—contribute additional variance in child EF, suggesting that both maternal cognitive capacity and behavioral interactions shape emerging regulatory skills through distinct pathways ref [40].

Conversely, emerging evidence suggests that individual differences in child EF may serve as a compensatory mechanism in the context of neurodevelopmental risk. In infants at familial risk for autism or ADHD, stronger EF skills may buffer against atypical neural development, reducing the likelihood of clinical diagnosis later in life ref [39]. This 'flip side' perspective reframes EF deficits not merely as core symptoms but as markers of failed compensation, highlighting EF as a potential target for early intervention. Caregivers who provide structurally supportive, responsive environments may foster EF growth that mitigates risk, particularly in genetically vulnerable populations.

subsections.subsection_title: Overlap and Distinction Between Autism and ADHD Symptomatology
subsections.content:
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) exhibit substantial symptom overlap, particularly in social-communicative difficulties and executive dysfunction, yet remain distinct in core phenotypic profiles. Population-based twin studies reveal that while ASD symptoms (social impairments, communication deficits, restricted interests) and ADHD symptoms (inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity) load onto separate latent factors, they share significant genetic influences, suggesting a common etiological substrate underlying their co-occurrence ref [41]. Latent class analyses in clinical and population samples further identify distinct subgroups, including children with predominant ADHD symptoms, those with dual clinical-level symptoms (ASD[+ADHD] and ADHD[+ASD]), and those with minimal symptoms, challenging the notion of a single overarching disorder ref [3]. Notably, while cognitive deficits in attention and motor variability are shared across comorbid groups, specific impairments in emotion recognition and detail-focused processing are more uniquely associated with ASD, supporting dimensional distinctions despite genetic overlap.

The pattern of symptom co-occurrence—where many children exhibit subthreshold features of one disorder alongside a primary diagnosis of the other—underscores the importance of moving beyond categorical diagnoses toward symptom-based phenotyping. This has implications for both clinical assessment, where dimensional approaches may better capture individual profiles, and molecular genetic research, where shared and distinct genetic variants can be more precisely mapped. Future research should integrate longitudinal behavioral data with neurocognitive and genetic markers to delineate early pathways that diverge toward ASD, ADHD, or their comorbid presentation.

subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Cognitive Markers of Autism and ADHD
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence from prospective longitudinal studies indicates that behavioral and cognitive markers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) can be detected in infancy, well before clinical diagnosis. In infants at familial risk for ASD, reductions in social orienting behaviors—such as gaze to faces, social smiling, and directed vocalizations—become evident by 12 months of age, with trajectories showing progressive decline rather than absence at birth ref [42]. Similarly, atypical visual attention, particularly delayed disengagement from central stimuli to peripheral targets, emerges by 14 months in infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis, suggesting a core deficit in attentional flexibility ref [44]. Contrary to early assumptions, infants at risk for ASD often show intact or even heightened initial orienting to faces, but fail to develop the adaptive modulation of this response over time ref [45]. For ADHD, early markers include motor and language delays, difficult temperament, and reduced head circumference growth as early as 3–18 months, with cognitive and behavioral indicators becoming distinguishable by 15–24 months, particularly in girls ref [43]. These markers are often subtle and show modest sensitivity in isolation, highlighting the need for multimodal assessment tools ref [33].

Notably, both disorders share overlapping early indicators such as atypical attention regulation and temperament profiles, yet diverge in the nature of social engagement: ASD is characterized by diminishing social motivation, while ADHD is marked by impulsivity and poor behavioral inhibition. The developmental trajectories of these markers suggest distinct neurocognitive pathways, with ASD involving disruptions in social orienting systems and ADHD involving broader regulatory and executive control deficits. Early identification of these markers may enable targeted interventions during critical windows of neuroplasticity, though current screening tools remain insufficiently sensitive for infancy and toddlerhood ref [43].

subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Trajectories and Endophenotypes in High-Risk Infants
subsections.content:
Longitudinal studies of high-risk infants—those with a sibling diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)—reveal distinct developmental trajectories that diverge from typical patterns as early as 14 months of age. Ref [2] demonstrated that infants later diagnosed with ASD exhibited significant declines in multiple developmental domains between 14 and 24 months, particularly in expressive and receptive language, fine motor, and gross motor skills, with the most pronounced deceleration occurring after the first birthday. These findings suggest a critical window of emerging disruption that precedes clinical diagnosis. Concurrently, fine motor delays in the first two years have been identified as a robust early predictor of later expressive language outcomes in high-risk infants, independent of ASD diagnosis, highlighting a shared developmental vulnerability ref [47].

Beyond motor and language domains, attentional processes serve as potential endophenotypes for neurodevelopmental risk. Ref [4] showed that focused attention at 7 months in preterm infants predicted later cognitive function and reduced hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms, suggesting that early attentional regulation may be a transdiagnostic endophenotype relevant to both ASD and ADHD. This aligns with the broader endophenotype framework, which posits that measurable, heritable, and trait-like intermediaries—such as attentional control, motor coordination, or language acquisition patterns—can bridge genetic risk and complex behavioral phenotypes ref [5]. In high-risk infant cohorts, these markers may reflect underlying neural inefficiencies that manifest differently across individuals, contributing to heterogeneous outcomes including ASD, language delay, or subclinical ADHD traits.

subsections.subsection_title: Developmental Trajectories and Growth Patterns Across Disorders
subsections.content:
Developmental trajectories in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) reveal distinct yet overlapping patterns of growth that inform early risk identification and long-term outcomes. In ADHD, persistent symptoms into adulthood are associated with atypical trajectories of cortical thinning, particularly in the medial and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, with each additional symptom correlating with accelerated thinning rates (ref [49]). Children who remit from ADHD exhibit cortical thickening or minimal thinning, suggesting a normative developmental catch-up, whereas those with persistent symptoms show fixed deficits. Prenatal and postnatal growth patterns also predict ADHD symptom severity, with smaller head circumference, lower birth weight, and reduced body-mass index from gestation through 56 months consistently linked to higher symptom scores, indicating a lack of catch-up growth as a potential neurodevelopmental risk marker (ref [50]).

In ASD, early growth trajectories diverge markedly, with accelerated head circumference growth emerging as a robust early biomarker. Infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis often exhibit abrupt increases in head circumference by 9 months, preceding observable behavioral symptoms and enabling early risk stratification (ref [5]). This pattern contrasts with the more gradual and linear growth trajectories observed in typically developing infants and those at risk for other neurodevelopmental delays. Together, these findings underscore that both disorders are characterized by non-linear, time-sensitive developmental pathways—ADHD by progressive cortical maturation deficits and ASD by early overgrowth in neuroanatomical size—highlighting the need for disorder-specific developmental models in early intervention planning.

subsections.subsection_title: White Matter and Connectivity Abnormalities in ASD and ADHD
subsections.content:
Emerging neuroimaging evidence highlights distinct white matter (WM) and structural connectivity abnormalities in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), suggesting divergent neurodevelopmental pathways. In ADHD, probabilistic diffusion tractography combined with graph theory analysis has revealed disrupted topological organization in whole-brain WM networks, particularly in regions supporting attentional control and executive function, with reduced global efficiency and altered small-world properties in drug-naive boys compared to typically developing peers ref [52]. These structural deficits may underlie the core behavioral symptoms of inattention and impulsivity, independent of pharmacological intervention.

In ASD, while structural connectivity findings are more heterogeneous, recent work emphasizes developmental trajectories of WM integrity, with early disruptions in long-range connections—particularly in the superior longitudinal fasciculus and corpus callosum—linked to social and communicative impairments ref [53]. Unlike ADHD, where WM abnormalities often reflect reduced integration, ASD may involve both hypo-connectivity in fronto-parietal networks and hyper-connectivity in local circuits, a pattern that evolves across childhood and adolescence. These divergent profiles suggest that while both disorders involve altered brain connectivity, their underlying neuroanatomical mechanisms and developmental trajectories differ significantly, warranting disorder-specific models of pathophysiology.

subsections.subsection_title: Early Behavioral and Temperamental Predictors of ADHD
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence indicates that behavioral and temperamental markers of ADHD can be detected in infancy and toddlerhood, preceding formal diagnosis by several years. Studies have identified difficult temperament, characterized by high irritability, low soothability, and poor regulatory capacity, as a robust early predictor of later ADHD symptoms, particularly when combined with motor and language delays ref [33]. Longitudinal analyses from the NICHD Study of Early Child Care and Youth Development reveal that children who later exhibit high levels of ADHD symptoms can be distinguished as early as 15 months in females and 24 months in males, based on parent-reported behavioral dysregulation and attentional difficulties, though sensitivity remains modest in early years ref [43].

Community-based pediatric assessments further support these findings, demonstrating that routine clinical observations—such as early attention problems, hyperactivity, absence of positive behaviors, and maternal smoking during pregnancy—significantly predict ADHD-related problems in adolescence, even in non-clinical populations ref [4]. These predictors are often compounded by sociodemographic risk factors, including lower maternal education and male sex, which consistently emerge across studies as amplifying vulnerabilities. Importantly, while individual markers show limited predictive power alone, their combination in multivariate models accounts for substantial variance in later ADHD outcomes, suggesting a polygenic and multifactorial developmental pathway.

subsections.subsection_title: Early Neuroanatomical Markers of Autism Spectrum Disorder
subsections.content:
Emerging evidence from prospective longitudinal studies indicates that neuroanatomical deviations in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are detectable in the first year of life, preceding overt behavioral symptoms. Infants who later receive an ASD diagnosis exhibit accelerated brain volume growth, particularly in cortical surface area and total brain volume, between 6 and 12 months of age, as revealed by serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in high-risk sibling cohorts ref [56]. This early overgrowth is accompanied by elevated extra-axial fluid, a finding that may reflect altered cerebrospinal fluid dynamics or impaired neural pruning ref [56]. However, the specificity of these markers has been challenged by recent analyses suggesting that apparent brain overgrowth relative to historical norms may reflect secular trends in population growth rather than disease-specific pathology ref [55]. A large community-based sample of over 75,000 children demonstrated similar head circumference trajectories to those previously labeled as 'overgrown' in ASD, raising questions about the validity of classical normative benchmarks ref [55].

Diffusion tensor imaging studies further reveal atypical trajectories in white matter microstructure, with infants who develop ASD showing elevated fractional anisotropy at 6 months followed by attenuated growth through 24 months, resulting in lower values by toddlerhood across multiple tracts including the corpus callosum and superior longitudinal fasciculus ref [6]. These alterations suggest disrupted myelination or axonal organization during a critical period of synaptic refinement. Early brain enlargement, as documented in cross-sectional and longitudinal MRI studies from birth to age 2, remains one of the most consistent neuroanatomical findings in ASD, though its heterogeneity across subgroups underscores the need for stratified analyses ref [9]. Together, these findings point to a dynamic, non-linear trajectory of brain development in ASD, with early structural deviations potentially serving as prodromal biomarkers when contextualized within normative developmental frameworks ref [55].
